stories.headline: Cowboys' season looks bleak but schedule offers some hope
stories.summary: Cowboys players and coaches are focused on a stretch of games versus teams that are struggling just like them.
stories.body:
FRISCO, Texas -- Quarterback Dak Prescott has been around long enough to know the general feeling around the Dallas Cowboys at the moment.

No one inside the organization -- ownership, personnel, coaches and players -- expected the team would be 2-4 after six games when they left Oxnard, California, at the end of training camp. They didn't expect the defense to be as porous as last year's, and certainly none of them expected the offense that returned nearly everybody from 2025 to be as inconsistent as it has been through six games.

"When your guys believe, you've got a chance," Prescott said following Sunday's 23-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers. "And we know right now that we're probably the only ones, the guys in the locker room are the only ones who do believe."

The rough start has led to the typical reaction from fans: owner and general manager Jerry Jones needs to hire a real general manager; coach Brian Schottenheimer is over his head; the effort is lacking. The fans could be put off by the 31-year Super Bowl drought or it could be recent failures.

The Cowboys had three straight 12-5 finishes from 2021 to 2023 but that seems a long time ago. It is as if the organization has not recovered from the 48-32 loss to the Packers in the wild-card round of the 2023 playoffs when a team that went undefeated at AT&T Stadium in the regular season was bludgeoned at home in the postseason.

Since then, the Cowboys are 16-23-1. While a good amount of the roster has been changed over -- only seven starters remain -- the success has disappeared.

Yet there is an opportunity for the Cowboys to get others to believe again, at least temporarily.

Five of the Cowboys' next six games, beginning with Monday's matchup against the similarly disappointing and 2-4 Philadelphia Eagles (8:15 p.m. ET, ABC/ESPN), are against teams with a combined 9-21 record. Only the San Francisco 49ers, who come to AT&T Stadium on Nov. 15, have a winning record (6-0).

The Cowboys play Philadelphia twice in that span, the second meeting coming on Thanksgiving. The Eagles have been hurt by retirement and decimated by injury, including quarterback Jalen Hurts being ruled out Monday for the remainder of the season due to blood clots in his lungs.

The Arizona Cardinals (Nov. 1) are 2-4 and coming off an upset win against the disappointing 2-4 Los Angeles Rams. The Cardinals have beaten the Cowboys four straight times but are hardly a vexing opponent. The Indianapolis Colts (Nov. 8) fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday. The Tennessee Titans (Nov. 22) are 1-5 and coming off their first win of the season.

But it's not about the Eagles, Cardinals, Colts or Titans. Nor is it about the 49ers.

"It's what's going on right here," cornerback DaRon Bland said. "I can't think about everything on the outside. I've got to think about what's right here and what we got in the room."

Last week, the Cowboys added Mike Pettine as a senior defensive assistant to aid first-time coordinator Christian Parker. Against the Packers, the Cowboys' defense had their first interception of the season, held Green Bay's run game in check (though it ranks even lower than the Cowboys) and had their first three-sack game of the season -- though they allowed 11 third-down conversions and seven pass plays of 15 yards or more.

The perplexing development has been the implosion of the offense with only 29 combined points over the past two games.

Schottenheimer said, "We have great trust in our offense." He added that the poor execution falls on the players and the coaches.

"I'm always honest with these guys. I raise my voice a lot with these guys," Schottenheimer said. "But again, how you get the message across to me is more about being upfront and honest and direct. And that's the way we talk, whether we win or we lose. And I think it's your responsibility as a head coach to paint the picture of why you either won or you lost."

Whether it's a paint-by-numbers or some sort of Picasso, the Cowboys hope the picture can change quickly.

"The answer is to win," left guard Tyler Smith said. "When you're losing, the only way you get out of a wreck like this is to win. And ultimately, I think winning just starts with being consistent with how you prepare. Ultimately, correcting the mistakes that you made.

"I feel like we're not playing our best ball right now. I don't think we're anywhere where we could be. I just feel like we just need to find a little bit more consistency with the way we play."

stories.headline: Raphinha: Barcelona defeat to PSG won't impact Clásico
stories.summary: Barcelona captain Raphinha doesn't expect the 4-2 defeat at Paris Saint-Germain that ended an 11-game winning run to affect their preparations for Sunday's Clásico showdown with Real Madrid.
stories.body:
Barcelona captain Raphinha doesn't expect the 4-2 defeat at Paris Saint-Germain that ended an 11-game winning run to affect their preparations for Sunday's Clásico showdown with Real Madrid.

"To be honest, we knew this could happen at some point -- suffering our first defeat," Raphinha told TNT Sports. "After all, we're playing against the two-time European champions on their home turf.

"We know how strong they are here. So, while we knew it was a possibility, we never stopped trying to find our own way of playing on the pitch...It was a balanced game.

"We knew it could happen, and well, at the end of the day, it's just three points lost -- no big deal. There are more games ahead."

Barça are six points clear of Madrid at the top of LaLiga.

"It's a difficult week, but I think we're well-prepared to face this week full of big matches," Raphinha said. "Our unbeaten run [in LaLiga] is still intact, and we'll do everything we can to keep it that way."

Raphinha returned to the starting XI against PSG after recovering from a thigh injury he had picked up during the recent international window. The Brazilian forward only played 60 minutes.

"The coach took me off, and I was a bit annoyed because I felt I could have kept going for a few more minutes," he said. "You always want to be out on the field, especially in a match of this magnitude. But it's all good.

- Anthony Gordon: PSG had better moments, more quality in Barcelona win

- How Raphinha's latest transformation made him into Barcelona's star striker

- Tired Barcelona undone by 'too many mistakes' as perfect start ends at PSG

"As I said, it's just another game; I'm still working on getting back to my best physically. Playing fewer minutes was part of the plan. But when a match like this ends, you just want to play again."

Raphinha believes Barcelona and PSG could both face each other in this season's Champions League final.

"The truth is, it could happen," he said. "Why not? After all, they are the two-time defending European champions, and we also have the goal of becoming champions ourselves.

"So, since both teams are contending for the Champions League title, there's a very strong possibility that we might cross paths."

stories.headline: VAR who incorrectly awarded Erling Haaland goal reinstated to Premier League
stories.summary: The VAR who incorrectly awarded Erling Haaland's Manchester derby goal last month has been reinstated to Premier League duty.
stories.body:
The VAR who incorrectly awarded Erling Haaland's Manchester derby goal last month has been reinstated to Premier League duty.

Matt Donohue, who along with assistant Blake Antrobus failed to spot Manchester City's Enzo Fernández was offside and interfering with play in the game at Old Trafford on Sept. 13, will be the assistant VAR at Saturday's match between Coventry and Fulham.

Donohue has not featured in any of the three match rounds since the incident. Antrobus made his first appearance since the derby as an assistant referee for the Newcastle vs. Aston Villa match last Saturday.

Pro Ref's chief refereeing officer Howard Webb said Donohue had developed "tunnel vision" in focusing on whether Haaland was in an offside position and added it was the job of the team around Donohue to help pull him out of that tunnel.

He has featured in the EFL since the derby and was the referee for the Championship match between Southampton and Bolton last Saturday and the Derby vs. Wrexham game on Oct. 10.

Meanwhile, the VAR recommendation to send off Brighton's Pascal Struijk in the match against Sunderland on Oct. 10 was backed by the Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel, despite Struijk's suspension later being removed for wrongful dismissal by an independent regulatory commission.

The five-person KMI panel, which is comprised of three former players and coaches, one Premier League representative and one from Pro Ref, disagreed with the on-field decision not to send off Struijk for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

- Football watchdog chair asserts 'absolute' power to force City sale

- Phil Foden: Still 'long way' from my best despite hat trick in Man City rout

- Enzo Maresca: Marc Guéhi is a future Manchester City captain

The panel backed the VAR recommendation to overturn the on-field decision and show a red card three to two.

The Premier League pointed out in publishing the KMI panel outcomes for match round six that the panel and the independent commission which quashed the suspension are entirely separate bodies with different purposes and processes.

stories.headline: The 5 biggest questions still facing Luka Doncic and the Lakers
stories.summary: After a transformative offseason on the floor and off, there are still massive unanswered questions for this Lakers team.
stories.body:
WITH LESS THAN 30 minutes until tipoff before the Los Angeles Lakers' preseason game against the Golden State Warriors last week, Luka Doncic was the only player on the court.

While both rosters readied themselves in the locker rooms at T-Mobile Arena, Doncic -- given the night off by Lakers coach JJ Redick -- used every bit of the hardwood for a basket-to-basket battle against three of L.A. assistant coaches.

In an exercise designed to tap into the mix of ferociousness and joy that Redick says is the optimal emotional plane for the 27-year-old star, Doncic was not given an inch by Lakers head video coordinator Michael Wexler.

The 5-foot-11 Wexler, a gritty guard who earned a spot on the Pepperdine basketball team, was armed with a foam-covered stick to bat at the arms and prod at the body of the six-time All-Star.

Lakers player development coach Justin Robinson -- standing 6-foot-9 with a sturdy frame, like his "Admiral" dad -- waited for the right time to crowd Doncic with a double team.

And then there was Lakers assistant coach Greg St. Jean, who, though he was technically on Doncic's team in case he needed to pass out of the double to reset the offensive possession, occasionally broke the rules and blitzed Doncic, too.

One trip down, Doncic tried a pull-up 3. The next, he got Wexler and Robinson to bite with a hesitation dribble and blew by them for a lay-in.

On another, he planted himself at the foul line and launched the one-legged fadeaway jumper that fueled the Hall of Fame career of his former Dallas Mavericks teammate Dirk Nowitzki.

After half-a-dozen full-court possessions, Doncic caught his breath and shot 45-foot bombs from the sideline.

When he airballed one, Wexler snickered.

"It's not an easy shot, OK?" Doncic barked back.

After the break, Doncic blazed down the left side of the court and veered back through the lane with a right-hand dribble when Wexler cut him off.

With all of his momentum taking him toward the sideline, Doncic put the ball in his left hand, extended that arm back toward the basket and flipped in a finger roll over Wexler's head, eliciting an "oooohhhh" from the hundreds of fans in the lower bowl.

After the bucket, Doncic flipped his middle finger in front of Wexler's face.

Retribution.

Lakers president of basketball operations and general manager Rob Pelinka watched all of this unfold from the bench, sitting next to Doncic's physiotherapist, Javy Barrio.

If it's the coaches' responsibility to motivate Doncic with creative drills like this 15-minute pregame gauntlet in Las Vegas, it's Barrio's job to keep him healthy, after a late-season hamstring injury sidelined him for the playoffs last spring.

Which leaves Pelinka tasked with building a team around Doncic's spectacular talent -- he secured the second scoring title of his career last season by topping 40 points 16 times -- that can contend for a championship.

Doncic's pregame display in Vegas left little doubt that he'll be as exciting as ever to watch this season.

But there are still major questions facing this Lakers team, with the season about to open Wednesday against the Warriors (7 p.m. PT, ESPN).

Doncic is undoubtedly the best player on the Lakers. But is he ready to lead them?
With LeBron James signed with the Philadelphia 76ers in free agency this summer, the pathway was cleared for Doncic to officially become the next face of the franchise.

His work began almost immediately.

He provided feedback to the front office as it built out the roster, notably requesting an "A-list center," sources told ESPN.

"When you can co-create something that's powerful with a star like Luka, and retrofit a team around him, then there's buy-in," Pelinka said last month. "We love those roundtable discussions where ideas are shared."

And then he footed the bill to host the entire team for a four-day minicamp and bonding trip in his hometown of Ljubljana, Slovenia, in August.

"I think there is a natural chemistry with this group that I think started over the summer," Redick said during training camp, crediting Doncic's role in fostering it. Doncic has given the team reason to believe in him.

He has maintained a workout and dietary regimen that resulted in an improved physique that he showed off on the cover of Men's Health in summer 2025.

"When you got a guy like Luka, going into the game you feel like you can beat anybody," Lakers backup center Kevon Looney said. "We feel like if we do our job, he's going to do his job and he's going to clinch us the game."

Redick told ESPN he already empowered Doncic to take control last season.

"There were really two dynamics for us," Redick told ESPN. "We like to use the term 'partnership.' I don't want him to view me as an authoritarian or anything like that. It's a partnership. It's open dialogue and all that stuff, which I think he likes.

"And then the second part ... your best offensive players should feel a level of freedom and a level of autonomy to be creative, but they've got to do that within the structure of the team and the offense."

Doncic, if he stays healthy, provides stable, star-level production. It's the rest of the roster where questions remain.

Do they belong in the championship conversation?
Doncic told ESPN's Brian Windhorst on media day that he believes the Lakers can win it all this season.

"I feel like I say this stuff a lot, but if you don't think we can win a championship, then you shouldn't be here," he said. "I'm always going to believe. If I don't believe, nobody believes. So I need to show that I believe -- which I honestly do -- and go from there."

Outside projections aren't as optimistic. ESPN's Basketball Power Index gives them just an 11% chance to make the Western Conference finals.

The competition -- from the champion New York Knicks and Western Conference champ San Antonio Spurs; to 2025 champion Oklahoma City Thunder; to other recent champs in the Boston Celtics and Denver Nuggets; to the revamped teams in Philadelphia, Minnesota and Miami -- is stiff.

But even leaving those teams out of it, is it realistic to bring up title talk?

Their new team not only has little experience together, but some key, new pieces have little experience on the sport's biggest stage. L.A.'s four big-ticket free agents in Walker Kessler (four years, $130 million), Quentin Grimes (four years, $60 million), Sandro Mamukelashvili (four years, $52 million) and Collin Sexton (two years, $27 million) have started just six playoff games in their careers combined.

Redick shares his star's confidence in the group, however.

"Unless somebody blatantly tells me that we're not trying to win, I think that every year," Redick said of his belief in the Lakers' chances. "I think because of our talent, because of our fit, because of our depth, I really like our team."

Is Walker Kessler enough to shore up their shoddy defense?
He'll certainly help.

L.A. mortgaged what was left of its future to land the 7-foot-2 big man, sending two unprotected future first-round picks and two pick swaps to the Utah Jazz in the deal.

"If you look at what you could potentially get in the draft or what is potentially going to come in free agency, those centers just don't exist," Pelinka said last month.

"So when the opportunity comes and you have a superstar like Luka in your building, you have to seize it. And we feel very comfortable and confident about that decision and what we put into it."

The Lakers were willing to pay the monumental price to fix their most pressing problem: their defense.

L.A. finished 20th in defense last season, allowing 115.5 points per 100 possessions, a regression from Redick's first year when the Lakers finished 17th.

The appeal of Kessler, 25, beyond being on the same career timeline as Doncic and the 28-year-old Austin Reaves, is his skill set, which should allow Redick to employ a base defense he is more comfortable with.

"We have the guys that can pick up full court and guard and be disruptive and then we have Walker back there," Redick said of this year's team, which also includes Sexton, Ziaire Williams and Matisse Thybulle.

The Lakers switched 40.6% of the time against on-ball screens in the last two seasons under Redick, the highest rate in the league over that time, according to GeniusIQ.

Kessler rarely played that way in Utah, switching only 10% of the time in his career against on-ball screens and playing in a drop scheme 52% of the time.

Kessler's 2.4 blocks per game career average is the second best in the league since 2022-23, behind only the Spurs' Victor Wembanyama.

And in that time, he also ranks in the top 10 in opponent field goal percentage among the 41 players to contest at least 2,000 shots within five feet of the basket, according to ESPN research.

"He's a great defensive player," Warriors coach Steve Kerr said of Kessler. "It's not very wise to go in and challenge him at the rim. ... He's one of the best rim protectors and one of the best defensive centers in the league."

The Lakers look different, but are they improved?
The Lakers are the first team in league history to win a playoff series and then lose all five starters from that group the following season.

James, Rui Hachimura, Marcus Smart, Luke Kennard and Deandre Ayton helped fuel the Lakers' late-season run: from the end of February through all of March, the team went 16-2 and looked like one of the best in the league.

Losing those players means losing a combined 59 years of experience, too.

"I don't want to compare the teams or the rosters, and I really have not thought about last year's team," Redick told ESPN.

Instead, Redick believes this roster features more optionality.

"What excites me about this roster is there are elements of modern basketball that we just haven't been able to do," Redick told ESPN. "Even with Smart, Smart at his age, can't pick up full court every single possession. And he was the only person that was even capable of doing that on our team last year to begin with. So just that alone, that's exciting.

"I think Walker has the potential to be one of the best rim [protection] guys, and when he's played, he's been that for the most part. ... So, it's more just being excited about this team, than comparing the two teams."

What is the backup backcourt situation?
Doncic and Reaves have already proved to be a dangerous backcourt pair, combining to average 56.8 points and 13.8 assists per game last season.

But they won't be on the court 48 minutes per game and, based on their recent injury history, they won't be in the lineup for all 82 games, either.

And with Sexton sidelined for all of the preseason with a right calf issue, Redick's other backcourt options have not performed well.

"That fourth ball handler for us hasn't been great," Redick said this past week.

This preseason, Jaden Hardy averaged 2.6 turnovers and 1.2 assists and shot 41% (30.4% from 3) in his 14.2 minutes per game; Bronny James averaged 2.4 turnovers and 2.8 assists and shot 25% (12.5% from 3) in 16.4 minutes per game; and two-way guard Chris Manon averaged 1.6 turnovers and 0.8 assists and shot 44.4% (25% from 3) in 12.4 minutes per game.

James, for his part, has been limited by a quad contusion he suffered just before the start of training camp, sources told ESPN, and Redick added that the third-year guard has often shared the court with training camp invitees, rather than rotation players and noted how James finished last season as a playoff contributor.

But the hole behind the Lakers' star backcourt could be the part of the roster Pelinka will have to fortify the most if the Lakers seriously plan to contend.

stories.headline: World Series opponents Brewers, Rays more different than you think
stories.summary: Yes, this Fall Classic is a battle of small-market teams that don't rely on home runs. But dig deeper, and you'll discover there's much more to this matchup.
stories.body:
Welcome to the small-market World Series. This is a theme you're likely to encounter a lot this week, as the momentum toward this Rays-Brewers showdown gathers.

To be sure, there are a number of similarities between the Brewers and Rays, but those similarities are mostly top-line items. The sub-traits beneath them are very different.

Take their markets, for example. They are small in different ways. By metro population figures and Major League Baseball's internal market score, Milwaukee is at the bottom of the league, while Tampa Bay ranks closer to the middle.

But if you look at revenue, their places flip. The Milwaukee metro area might be small, but the Brewers are a regional franchise that has fans all over Wisconsin.

It's a similar situation on the field. Both clubs have become known for pivoting away from the onslaught of strikeouts and home runs in today's game. But when you dig a bit deeper, it's clear they took different routes to get to the Fall Classic.

This series isn't alluring because of how the teams are alike, but how they are different. And this is why this promises to be a tremendously entertaining matchup between two legit No. 1 seeds, one in which two of the game's best managers -- Tampa Bay's Kevin Cash and Milwaukee's Pat Murphy -- might play outsized roles.

So how are they different?

Long ball liberation
This was the theme of a piece I wrote about the Brewers' offense at the outset of the playoffs. It isn't that Milwaukee is a small-ball offense; it's that the Brewers play like a small-ball offense when the situation warrants. But when they need to muscle up, they are able to do that. These aren't the 1980s Cardinals of Willie McGee and Vince Coleman, even if the Brewers also feature a second baseman who drove in 100 runs (Brice Turang, while Tom Herr did it for those St. Louis teams).

The key stat that will spur many to lump the Milwaukee and Tampa Bay offenses together is this: The Rays ranked 29th in percentage of runs coming via the homer, ahead of only the Brewers. This is indeed how they are most similar -- neither club relies on homers to score.

But while both teams have power, they have different strategies about when to emphasize it. The Rays ranked 13th in slugging with the bases empty, but 17th with men on base. The Brewers ranked 24th in slugging with the bases empty, but fifth with men on base. Similar results, different paths. For both clubs, it's truer to say that they don't rely on homers than to say they can't hit them.

During the playoffs, both teams have featured more or less balanced offenses, at least in relation to the rest of the playoff field. The Brewers have scored via the long ball 35% of the time; the Rays are at 31%, both below the overall playoff average of 38%. Both rank in the top half of playoff teams in runs per game both with, and without, home runs.

Hitting with the bases empty
Both teams hit .258 during the regular season, with the Brewers topping the majors once you go out a fourth decimal point. Batting averages! Old school approaches! Yes, but the routes these offenses take to the same average could hardly be more different. Once again, we can see this vividly in how the offenses approach bases-empty situations.

With no one on base, the Brewers had by far the lowest swing rate in the majors (42.5%); the Rays were 15th (47.1%). The Brewers saw the most pitches in those spots (4.07 pitches per plate appearance); the Rays were 28th (3.82). The Rays had the second-best rate of putting the ball in play (78.2%), while the Brewers had the second-best BABIP (.306).

The Rays are all about ambushing early in the count, especially with no one on base, which in part translates to their high slugging percentage in those situations even though their overall hard-hit rate is nearly at the bottom of the majors. The Brewers, on the other hand, grind. When no one is on base, the top priority is to change that and get to first base.

Hitting with runners on base
Here we're talking about the ability to alter approaches with runners on base. These are the two best teams in the majors at doing this. The Brewers led the majors with an RBI rate of 18.9% (percentage of runners on base driven in); the Rays were second at 18.1%.

The difference in their success rates means the Brewers drove in 73.1 runs above expectation, while the Rays were at 45.1.

So these are the two best teams at cashing in their baserunners, but once again, there are differences in how they do this. The Rays get even more aggressive, with their rock-bottom pitches-per-plate-appearance figure dropping to 3.69. They put the ball in play but do so with the lowest isolated power figure (.135) in the majors. The Brewers, on the other hand, remain patient, but their slugging and isolated power indicators go up, as does their home run rate.

If there is a lesson here for other teams when it comes to succeeding in RISP situations, it might lie in another common trait between the Rays and Brewers: swing path. The Brewers hit the ball harder more often than the Rays, who seem to actually favor lower exit velocities in their style of play, at least for some of their players. But however the ball comes off the bat, for both of these teams it's likely to come in the form of a grounder or line drive. The Rays (29th) and Brewers (30th) have the two lowest average launch angles in baseball.

Speed
Both clubs are full of plus runners who pressure opposing defenses on the bases and run down balls in the field.

The Rays ranked second in steals and steal attempts per opportunity; the Brewers were fifth and sixth in those columns. They were both successful around 75% of the time, with the Rays ranking 18th and the Brewers 19th. Thus, both clubs are willing to accept a few caught stealing when it comes to pressuring the opponent.

This similar penchant for derring-do on steals doesn't translate to running the bases in general, though. The more-aggressive Rays took the extra base 42% of the time, right at the MLB average, while the Brewers were at 41%. Still, only three teams made more outs while running the bases than Tampa Bay (54); the Brewers were tied for 21st (28).

Pitching
These are two of the best pitching staffs in baseball and two of the best at overall run prevention. In the playoffs, the Rays' rotation has outperformed every other team's starters, largely because of how hot Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta have gotten.

The Brewers have gotten less from their starters, but the dominance of their bullpen has been one of the postseason's leading narratives. Runs will be hard to come by in the World Series.

There are stark differences in collective emphasis between the two staffs. The Brewers led the majors in strikeout rate; the Rays led in walk rate. Perhaps due to their focus on strike-throwing, the Rays were more susceptible to the long ball. If Milwaukee is able to power up situationally as I've suggested, this might be the series to do so.

In terms of the rate of pitches in the zone, Milwaukee actually ranked higher (second) than Tampa Bay (third). The Rays get away with being in the zone so much because they allowed the third-lowest exit velocity this season and the lowest opposing BABIP. The Brewers do it by missing bats.

The real difference that will jump out is the Rays' much-touted use of the changeup, by far the highest usage in the majors. The Brewers led the majors in hard stuff -- two-seamers, four-seamers, cutters.

Two great pitching staffs with very different approaches against two contrasting styles of offense. It's a seamhead's dream matchup.

Home-field edge
The Rays and Brewers tied for the MLB lead with 55 home wins during the regular season. They are a combined 8-1 at home during the postseason. One difference between these similar levels of home dominance is attendance -- the Brewers drew almost twice as many fans per game during the regular season. Based on what we saw in the ALCS, this won't be in effect in the World Series. Both venues will be loud and jam-packed.

Still, there are differences here. I have a home reliance metric that looks at how much of a team's overall run differential is based on its play at home. It's expressed as an index, and Milwaukee's 125 tied with the Chicago White Sox for the highest in baseball. The Rays were more middle-of-the-pack at 104.

The disparity comes at the plate. Milwaukee's 5.52 runs per game at American Family Field were considerably more than any team. The Brewers' offense was still good on the road, ranking sixth at 4.75. The Rays were 13th in home scoring and 15th on the road. Of course, it should be noted that while these numbers explain Milwaukee's greater degree of home reliance, its offense performed better than the Rays through either prism.

Managers
Cash and Murphy have both won two Manager of the Year awards. Murphy is likely to win a third straight this season. Cash has a chance at his third, too, though Chicago's Will Venable is probably the AL favorite. Still, it adds up to the same thing: These are two of baseball's elite managers, perhaps its two best.

It's hard to really capture the differences between managers with trackable strategy preferences because managing is so much more than that. Both rank near the top of the majors in calling for steals and bunts, and they pinch run more than anyone. Cash is about twice as likely to call for an intentional walk. But the real differences here are more ephemeral, subjective and based on impressions.

Cash is a bona fide skipper who is empowered to run his team as he sees fit. He's an extension of the Rays' cutting-edge front office in that he has such a firm grasp of analytics and probability that he is able to seamlessly factor that data into his decision-making. Because he's a participant in those processes and not a puppet, he's the ideal 21st century manager, especially for a low-payroll team such as the Rays that needs to play every edge.

Murphy's front office is as innovative as any team, with the Rays perhaps being the only exception. But to hear Murphy tell it, he can't count to 10 without using his fingers. It's a put-on of course because that's what Murphy does: He raises self-deprecation to an art form. But there is no question that Murphy doesn't fixate on numbers.

What I mean by that is the actual numbers, not the stories they tell. Murphy can't tell you what Jackson Chourio's batting average is, much less his exit velocity. But he does have a preternatural grasp of baseball concepts honed over time at every level of the game. It's not that Murphy doesn't listen to his front office, it's that he's able to internalize the information he's given and then channel the takeaways toward his clubhouse and his coaches in an unmistakably Murphy-esque manner.

The approaches are different and they've both worked spectacularly.

Star power
What is stardom in baseball? Is it media attention and/or celebrity? Or is it being really good at baseball? Let's focus on the latter.

In terms of my true talent ratings, there will be 11 top 100 players in the series. The Brewers feature six, including No. 5 Jacob Misiorowski and No. 6 Turang. The Rays have five, led by No. 11 Junior Caminero and No. 13 Rasmussen. The MLB median for top 100 players on a team is three.

These teams might not have baseball's most famous rosters, Misiorowski aside, but both are laden with top-flight, baseball-playing stars. That ultimately is where I want to leave you. These teams are young, talented, deep, athletic and good at every facet of the game. They are the two best teams in baseball, each vying for the first title in franchise history.

All right, so maybe this is one example of how their similarities make the series more alluring than their differences do. Either way, this is the best possible World Series matchup the 2026 season could have given us. Relish it.

stories.headline: Atlanta Dream rookie Madina Okot staying ready for her call in WNBA Finals
stories.summary: Atlanta Dream rookie Madina Okot says she is staying ready, and preparing for whenever her name is called to help her team win the WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries.
stories.body:
Atlanta Dream rookie Madina Okot says she is staying ready, and preparing for whenever her name is called to help her team win the WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries.

Okot made her first Finals appearance in Atlanta's 79-65 Game 2 victory at Chase Center on Monday which leveled the best-of-seven series at 1-1 and gave the Dream their first ever Finals win going into Game 3 at State Farm Arena in Atlanta on Wednesday.

After remaining on the bench throughout the 68-64 loss in Game 1, the Kenyan center was called in and played 37 seconds late in the first quarter of Game 2. She committed a traveling violation just before star Angel Reese returned, finishing without a shot attempt or rebound.

"I don't think getting on the floor is going to be very hard for me because I believe that is what I am here for," Okot told Nigerian journalist Femi Adefeso.

"I am staying ready and I am going to be ready when my name is called. If I get the opportunity I am going to go out there and do my best to help my team win."

Okot appeared in 42 regular-season games for Atlanta, making two starts and averaging 5.4 points and 3.3 rebounds in 9.1 minutes per game. She shot 58% from the field and 76.8% from the free-throw line.

"It's been great. I am still young. I'm a rookie, I'm learning," she said. "It's a very important experience in my basketball journey moving forward. The roles are just different, its about knowing the role. I am staying ready and doing what I am supposed to do."

Atlanta selected the 6-foot-6 centre 13th overall out of South Carolina in April, and among the lessons she is learning in her rookie season is mental toughness, something that Atlanta seem to have in abundance.

Her teammates' performances in Game 2 offered examples that she says she is learning from.

After a less than stellar performance, Reese took responsibility after going scoreless in the second half of the Finals opener, saying she had let her team down. She responded with 30 points and 16 rebounds to lead Atlanta to their Game 2 victory.

Rhyne Howard also overcame foul trouble to set a Finals record with six steals. Jordin Canada contributed 10 assists despite shooting 3 for 14 from the field, finishing with 13 points. Okot pointed to the mental fortitude of her teammates, as some of the biggest lessons she is learning in Atlanta.

"It's just being tough mentally and being willing to learn everyday," she said. "It's great being around the greatest players in the world and competing against them. That's going to be so big in my journey."

Okot has reached the WNBA Finals just six years after taking up basketball. Raised in Mumias, Kenya, she grew up playing volleyball before switching sports at 16. She played at Mississippi State before transferring to South Carolina for her final college season and she says she is not taking the opportunity for granted.

"It feels great to be in the WNBA Finals. I am so grateful for this opportunity," she said. "It is an exciting feeling, I am just proud of the hard work I have put in to get to where I am today."

That hard work has not gone unnoticed. It led to a visit from Kenyan President William Ruto, who watched Atlanta beat the New York Liberty 83-65 in September while he was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.

"That was amazing. I was so excited once I heard that he was coming," she said. "That was so big for me. It just shows how much he appreciates sports and I hope that is going to open a lot of doors for young girls back home and that will also help grow the game back home."

Circuit of the Americas

The Circuit of the Americas first hosted the United States Grand Prix in 2012, to mark the end of a five year wait since the race at Indianapolis.

Mario Andretti, who won the world championship in 1978, opened the track and it has become a popular race among drivers and fans alike with plenty of overtaking action and drama.

COTA is a varied circuit with straights, esses through to sector two, and a series of hair-pins in sector three. The high-speed corners takes some inspiration from Silverstone and Hockenheim.

It's a mix of fast corners, long straights and has one of the steepest elevation climbs to Turn 1.

Who will win this year?

Antonelli will be as focused as ever to claim his ninth victory of the season with one hand already on the drivers' championship trophy.

However, Mercedes are still working on how to best optimise its current upgrade package. Last time out in Singapore, the team ran Russell on the older specification, while Antonelli had the upgraded package.

Red Bull were labelled by rivals as the "team to beat" for the remaining six races of the season. There seems to be no stopping Verstappen, who has won the U.S. Grand Prix four times.

Don't count out Hamilton who holds the record for six wins around COTA and will be looking to get his seventh podium for Ferrari this season.

stories.headline: Consensus top AFL draft prospect Dougie Cochrane already in rare air
stories.summary: Missing significant chunks of football hasn't stopped Port Adelaide NGA star Dougie Cochrane from firming as the top prospect in this year's AFL draft.
stories.body:
It's rare for a player to be the consensus no. 1 rated prospect in their draft. From coaches to recruiters and a myriad of draft evaluators, Dougie Cochrane stands atop 2026's crop. For him to do so after playing just four games in his top-age campaign puts the Port Adelaide NGA gun in rare air.

The starring junior missed both years of his u18 national championships through injury, and this year only returned to the field in the final month of the season. But what he produced at league level last season and amongst his peers at the u16s national championships in 2024 is not easily forgotten.

Clearly a class above at the national championships three years ago, Cochrane put all of his skill and athleticism on show. He was a distributor out of defence, won aerial duels around the ground and was the focal point of the SA forward line in a showing of his unique versatility.

From there he made his league debut for Central Districts as a 17-year-old, kicking four goals including an outrageous snap on his left foot from the pocket after crumbing a forward 50 contest. From his first game he was already the best player on the ground.

Speaking to ESPN ahead of the draft combine Cochrane was a bit flat. It wasn't because he'd missed his top-age season, he knew he wasn't going to be testing, and he knew most clubs wouldn't bother booking an interview given his ties to Port Adelaide. But there was one thing that really got to him.

"They measured me at 194-and-a-half centimetres," he tells ESPN with a grin. "They took a centimetre off me, but we'll round that up."

At six-foot-four (we'll round it up too) he's widely considered the next elite key forward prospect to come through the AFL Draft. Only he doesn't necessarily see it that way.

"I want to be a midfielder when I'm older, that's what I'm striving towards. "For right now I'm pretty happy forward, if not back. I'm happy wherever the team needs, whatever the team needs.

"I'm pretty skinny right now, I'm not as muscly as the Patty Cripps's of the world, the Bonts of the world. I want to focus on my midfield craft and get that experience."

Cochrane missed a significant chunk of his bottom-age year with a hamstring and over the off-season underwent knee surgery to address patella tendinitis. He didn't play for 11 straight months from the end of 2025 to July 2026.

Watching from the sidelines frustrated him but he knew it was all out of an abundance of caution.

"I started playing league at Centrals last year, I sort of started feeling [knee pain] a little bit. I thought nothing of it, just thought it was a bit of growing pain. It got worse and worse by the time I started doing pre-season... when you take off and do your powerful stuff it flares up.

"They did a clean out of it... I had the surgery, and I walked out of the surgery. It was two little key holes."

Cochrane sat down with ESPN as Port Adelaide list manager Jason Cripps all but confirmed on Trade Radio Essendon would be bidding on the gun academy prospect at pick one in the 2026 AFL Draft.

He's the son of Port Adelaide and North Melbourne midfielder Stuart Cochrane, and grew up supporting the Power after his dad's playing career finished up. His brother Tom was on the list during formative years and the club is set up to match his bid wherever it lands.

"Dad's been my idol growing up. Looking up to him, I obviously didn't get to see him play but he's been enormous."

Asked if it would mean more being that first selection on November 19, Cochrane's humble nature shines through.

"I loved watching the draft growing up, seeing those high picks. The pick doesn't really matter, does it? There have been a lot of picks over times where the number one picks haven't gone as well as they should've. I just want to end up at an AFL club - wherever that is I don't mind - but I just want to play footy," he says.

"Growing up and supporting Port all my life, it would be special playing for them. But whatever happens happens and I'm just gonna let that decide itself."

stories.headline: A global experiment: Can ESPN predict the Ballon d'Or awards?
stories.summary: The Ballon d'Or awards are typically tough to predict, but can ESPN and our global resources do just that?
stories.body:
The destination of the Ballon d'Or is typically tough to predict. Just ask Real Madrid's Vinícius Júnior, who, in 2024, had spent weeks believing he would win the men's award only to learn hours ahead of the ceremony that it had gone to Manchester City midfielder Rodri instead.

This year, it is no less straightforward.

On the men's side, there are plenty of candidates: Teenager Lamine Yamal dazzled for Barcelona, Harry Kane scored more goals for Bayern Munich than he ever has before, Kylian Mbappé starred for Real Madrid, while the 2026 World Cup saw Lionel Messi and Rodri compete to be named the competition's best player (in the end, it went to Rodri).

And for the Ballon d'Or Féminin, Alexia Putellas is the favorite after captaining Barcelona to another quadruple, but she was far from the only world-class player on that team.

The winners for both will be revealed on Oct. 26 at a glitzy ceremony in London, alongside a number of other awards, but is there a way to gauge who will walk away with the prizes ahead of time?

The men's Ballon d'Or is decided by a group of 100 journalists, each from different countries, while the Ballon d'Or Feminin's voting roll is made up of 50 journalists from 50 different countries. We decided to replicate that voting with ESPN journalists stationed all over the world.

Here's how we did it:

Methodology:

ESPN has a global team of journalists in every corner of the globe. We asked 20 ESPN journalists from around the world -- one per country -- to submit a ballot.
We used the official Ballon d'Or shortlists.
We had each voter submit their top five for the Ballon d'Or and their top three for all other awards.
Like official awards, each first-place vote received 15 points, followed by 12 points for second, 10 points for third, eight points for fourth and six points for fifth.

So, in a global experiment, can ESPN predict the Ballon d'Or?

Jump to:

Ballon d'Or | Women's Ballon d'Or

Other awards

BALLON D'OR: PLAYERS WHO GOT 1ST-PLACE VOTES

Lamine Yamal, Barcelona, RW

What our voters said:

Josué Utrilla, ESPN Guatemala reporter: "I believe that being a world champion -- while playing a key role in Spain's attack and enjoying excellent form with Barcelona in LaLiga -- demonstrates the talent he possesses at such a young age (19) and has earned him a place among football's biggest stars."

Harry Kane, Bayern Munich, ST

What our voters said:
Tom Hamilton, ESPN UK senior writer: "Okay, he didn't win the World Cup, or the Champions League, but Kane's year is unsurpassed. He scored 73 goals in 65 matches across the England national team and Bayern. It's a freakish record, the like of which we'll never see again. Let's park sentimentality and aesthetic-influenced bias; this award rewards individual brilliance."

Thijs Zwagerman, ESPN NL reporter: "Despite scoring goals at an extraordinary rate for years, Kane still does not receive the full recognition he deserves on the international stage. His qualities extend far beyond his remarkable goal-scoring record. He possesses the rare ability for a striker to drop deep, influence the game from a deeper position and operate like a playmaker as well. While Kane has yet to win the Champions League or the World Cup, that does not diminish his individual brilliance. In my view, he was still the best player in the world on an individual level."

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami CF, FW

What our voters said:
Anirudh Menon, ESPN India editor: "If this award is to be given to the best footballer on the planet, there can only be one answer. He may be 39 years old; he may even be playing in Major League Soccer (where he did win the MLS Cup and topped almost every attacking chart in the league), but the 2026 World Cup showed just how vast the gulf between Messi and everyone else remains. When he turns it on, there isn't anyone close. Give him his ninth Ballon d'Or already."

Teo Coquet, ESPN Argentina reporter: "I choose him because of his attacking influence and ability to remain decisive on the international stage. His performance for Argentina at the World Cup is also a key factor in my evaluation. At 39 years old, he has played one of the best World Cups of his career."

Kylian Mbappé, Real Madrid, ST

What our voters said:

Omar Flores, ESPN Mexico reporter: "Mbappé was the leading scorer across every competition he played in during the 2025-26 season, topping the charts in both the UEFA Champions League and Spain's LaLiga. At the World Cup, the France star scored 10 goals and became the tournament's all-time leading scorer (22 goals). Although he was unable to help his team advance beyond the semifinals, he remains one of the leading candidates to win the Ballon d'Or. "

Carlos Valdez, ESPN Colombia reporter: "I would put Mbappé first because of his extraordinary ability to make the difference at the highest level. His pace, finishing, consistency and capacity to deliver in decisive moments make him one of the most influential players in world football. His goal-scoring achievements across the league, Champions League and World Cup further strengthen his case. For me, the Ballon d'Or should recognize not only outstanding numbers, but also a player's ability to change the course of a game, and Mbappé embodies that quality."

Fabián Ruiz, Paris Saint-Germain, CM

What our voters said:

Moises Llorens, ESPN Spain reporter: "If we forget about the cameras, the spotlights, the commercial interests, and all the pomp that increasingly accompanies the business of football, then Ruiz should win the Ballon d'Or. I have no doubt about it. Why? It's simple. He was an undisputed and fundamental player for PSG's repeated Champions League title success last season, and was equally fundamental for Luis de la Fuente's victorious Spain side at the 2026 World Cup when Pedri wasn't at his best in midfield. Ruiz won it all over the past 12 months and was a standout player. He lacks marketing appeal, which will work against him, but he would be a deserving winner."

Rodri, Barcelona, CM

What our voters said:

Jean Beausejour, ESPN Chile analyst: "In a World Cup year, winning the tournament carries enormous weight. Rodri had a tremendous influence on Spain's performances on football's biggest stage. Spain's ability to dominate matches, control the tempo and impose their style of play against different opponents was largely down to Rodri's intelligence, positioning and exceptional ability to dictate the game. His influence went far beyond individual statistics, making him, in my opinion, the most deserving candidate for the Ballon d'Or."

ESPN'S PREDICTED WINNER: HARRY KANE

In a symbol of how divisive the men's Ballon d'Or race is, Kane received half of the first-place votes but only one of the other 10 voters put him second. Perhaps the biggest surprise was the large snubbing of Yamal, who received just a single No. 1 vote.

This was a two-horse race and, as ESPN writer Bill Connelly wrote earlier this month: "Kane played eight more matches and over 600 more minutes than Yamal -- which is to say, he stayed healthier than a player 14 years his junior -- and he produced 81 combined goals and assists, a full 36 more than Yamal."

There is a slice of history on offer for Kane, too: Kane would be just the fifth Englishman to cradle the golden trophy, alongside Sir Stanley Matthews, Sir Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen.

BALLON D'OR FEMININE: PLAYERS WHO GOT 1ST-PLACE VOTES
Alexia Putellas, London City Lionesses, AM

What our voters said:

Leonard Solms, ESPN Africa reporter: "In her final season at Barcelona, midfield maestro Putellas not only captained Barcelona to the Liga F, UEFA Women's Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de España trophies -- but also scored 20 goals and assisted 14 in 43 games. Capable of filling multiple roles in the team, Putellas is the kind of player any manager would love to have 11 of, and her brilliance should not be taken for granted."

Marissa Lordanic, ESPN Australia editor: "Putellas was once again invaluable across multiple competitions. The epitome of a big-game player, she ensured Barcelona's trophy case continued to grow before she tested herself in a new league."

Ewa Pajor, Barcelona, ST

What our voters said:

Gustavo Hofman, ESPN Brasil reporter: "Pajor combined outstanding individual production with collective success and delivered when it mattered most. She recorded 34 goals and eight assists in 46 appearances for club and country, helping Barcelona win the Champions League, Liga F, Copa de la Reina and Spanish Super Cup. Her intelligent movement and clinical finishing gave Barcelona a cutting edge throughout the season, but her Champions League performances ultimately put her ahead of the competition: she finished as the tournament's top scorer with 11 goals and scored twice in the 4-0 victory over OL Lyonnes in the final."

Ed Dove, ESPN Africa reporter: "In recent years, Pajor's performances haven't always been rewarded with the silverware and honors one might expect. That changed last term, where she was a key influence -- and a major goal threat -- in Barcelona's historic Quadruple-winning campaign. A genuine big-game player, she scored 33 across all competitions, including 11 in the Champions League, where she struck in every knockout round Barca played in before netting twice in a one-sided final victory over OL Lyonnes. Pajor may have scored fewer than she did during his remarkable debut season at Barca, but after overcoming the UWCL final defeat by Arsenal in 2025, she deserves the individual recognition here."

Temwa Chawinga, Kansas City Current, FW

What our voters said:

Jeff Kassouf, ESPN (US) reporter: "No player changes a game like Chawinga. She can create chances on her own in one-vs.-one situations from literally inside her own half on the counter attack, and is a sharp goal scorer. Scoring 20 goals in the NWSL and then following that up with 15 the next season is dominant form at a world-class level. And she does it for club and country, having helped lowly Malawi to the 2027 World Cup. This time next year, more international opponents will know the fear of having Chawinga run at their defense."

Patri Guijarro, Barcelona, CM

What our voters said:

Moises Llorens, ESPN Spain: "The backbone of Barcelona's women's team and an excellent midfielder who makes runs from the second line. Other players usually steal the spotlight, but her talent is unquestionable. She makes the rest of the team shine."

ESPN'S PREDICTED WINNER: ALEXIA PUTELLAS
This result is not a surprise. Putellas is the clear favourite for the award, and our voters agreed.

Putellas enjoyed a dream end to her 14-year Barcelona career last season, captaining the club to a second Quadruple in three years, including lifting the Women's Champions League, before she moved to captain London City Lionesses, who are now third in the Women's Super League after five games.

Should Putellas actually win, she would earn her third Ballon d'Or award, joining former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmatí as its most frequent recipient.

The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Panthers lock in Patea
Penrith have secured Tua Patea until the end of 2029, with the youngster signing an extension that includes a pathway from a development contract into the club's top 30.

Patea capped off the 2026 season with a hat-trick in the Panthers' Jersey Flegg Grand Final victory, having started the year with an NRL training block.

The new deal will see him join Penrith's full-time NRL squad as he works towards a first-grade debut.

Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return

Jeral Skelton is closing in on a return to Canterbury following his departure from the Wests Tigers.

ESPN understands the Bulldogs are in advanced discussions to bring the outside back to the club for the 2027 season.

An agreement is understood to be close, although the deal has yet to be finalised.

Multiple NRL sides eye Knights forward

A Sydney club and a Queensland-based club are monitoring Newcastle forward Mat Croker ahead of November 1.

ESPN understands the two clubs have shown interest in the 27-year-old, who is approaching the final year of his Knights contract and can negotiate with rivals for 2028 onwards from next month.

Rivals keeping tabs on Dragons' Tu

Multiple clubs are monitoring St George Illawarra outside back Setu Tu, with the Dragons yet to begin talks over a contract extension.

Tu is contracted until the end of 2027 and is expected to test the open market from November 1, when rival clubs can negotiate a deal for 2028 and beyond.

The former Warriors outside back joined the Dragons on a development contract this season and is set to move into the club's top 30 squad in 2027.

His ability to cover multiple positions across the backline adds to his appeal as clubs assess their recruitment options.

Rivals monitor Patea as open market looms
Penrith young gun Luron Patea is expected to test the open market from November 1, with multiple clubs keeping tabs on the promising prop.

Patea is contracted until the end of 2027, but the Panthers are yet to begin talks over an extension, leaving rival clubs poised to explore a deal for 2028 and beyond.

Penrith have not granted Patea permission to negotiate with other clubs before November 1.

The Panthers junior made his NRL debut in 2024 and has shown promise during his first-grade opportunities, providing another emerging option in Penrith's forward pack.

He is among several Panthers players approaching the final year of their contracts, with veteran prop Moses Leota also unsigned beyond 2027.

Roosters eye Dockar-Clay reunion
The Roosters have shown interest in a potential return for Zach Dockar-Clay as they explore options to bolster their hooking and utility depth.

ESPN understands the 31-year-old has emerged as an option following his departure from Manly, with discussions remaining at an early stage.

Dockar-Clay spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons with the Roosters before joining the Sea Eagles on a one-year deal for 2026.

Manly confirmed his departure last month after a season in which he claimed the club's NSW Cup best-and-fairest award.

Bostock brushes Dragons links

Dolphins star Jack Bostock has dismissed recent links between himself and the Dragons, admitting this isn't the first time he'd been floated for a club switch.

"I've been linked to a few a clubs," Bostock admitted.

"I don't know about [the Dragons links]."

He said that while he "obviously sees it in the media," his sole focus is the Kangaroos.

Sloan's Dragons stay still a possibility

Tyrell Sloan could yet remain at St George Illawarra next season, with discussions ongoing over a potential stay despite his planned move to Castleford.

There is interest in keeping Sloan at the Dragons, but several hurdles remain before that can become a reality.

Roster space and salary cap room would need to be worked through, while any arrangement would also require Castleford to agree to release him.

Sloan previously admitted he would "love to" remain in the NRL when speaking to Channel Nine in August, after his Castleford deal had been announced.

No agreement has been reached and a stay is far from guaranteed.

stories.headline: NFL Week 7 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we're hearing
stories.summary: Will the Seahawks stick with Sam Darnold past this season? Could Vita Vea get trade interest? What's next for the NFC East teams? And could the Colts make more changes?
stories.body:
Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season has arrived. Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

What does the future hold for Bo Nix, Jalen Hurts, C.J. Stroud and other quarterbacks with looming contract situations? Who are some players that might be flying under the radar as trade candidates ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline? Will the Colts -- who just fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday -- keep making changes as they try to right the ship? And which of the NFC East teams in flux are most likely to shake things up in the coming weeks?

It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 7.

Jump to:

QB situations | Colts' next moves

Sneaky trade candidates

NFC East shake-ups | Fantasy advice

What is the most intriguing quarterback contract situation for the offseason?
Graziano: I recognize that there are far more important real-life situations going on around this player right now, but for me, it's the Eagles' Jalen Hurts. He is signed through 2028, but the only guaranteed money left on his contract after this year will be $22 million of his $51.5 million salary in 2027. Regardless of how this season was to play out for Hurts and the Eagles, there was always going to be an offseason discussion about whether to extend him again -- and if so, at what level -- or look into other options.

The Eagles have some young stars coming up for extensions pretty soon, including cornerbacks Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean, and carrying a huge quarterback salary beyond this year is going to get more difficult. It's fair to wonder what impact Hurts being out for the rest of the season will have on the Eagles' decision-making.

Fowler: Hurts belongs high on the list, as it's worth wondering whether he has played his last down as an Eagle. He is 59-28 as a starter for the franchise, but Philadelphia, which is often proactive with contracts of core players, did not extend Hurts last offseason. So, it's difficult to pinpoint where things will stand three to four months from now.

But my pick is the Broncos' Bo Nix. Denver is good enough to keep winning despite Nix showing a limited ceiling. He is a quality starter but is not poised to enter the upper echelon. Confidence appears to be an issue this season, raising questions about what this player-team marriage looks like long term.

To be sure, the conditions around Nix aren't perfect. Denver is struggling to run the ball and effectively create explosive plays off play-action. He has had two playcallers this season. Nix got skewered for last week's performance versus Seattle. But Denver didn't have as big of a problem with it because it had to play conservatively in a tight game between two great defenses, as whichever team won the turnover battle was probably going to win the game. Broncos coach Sean Payton knew that and most certainly relayed it to Nix, whose struggles against the 49ers in Week 4 were considered more problematic. That said, Nix doesn't appear to be the runner he once was. His viability with Denver might hinge on how he plays over the next 11 or so games.

Graziano: I did have someone last week tell me the big difference with Nix was that he's not getting himself out of bad spots with his legs the way he did last season but that he doesn't look much different otherwise. But that lack of running is a big deal, and if it doesn't improve, we could be left watching his flaws the rest of the way.

I'm a bit curious about Sam Darnold's situation, as he'll have one year left on his contact after this season. He is scheduled to make $35.5 million in 2027, but none of that money is guaranteed. There is a $10 million roster bonus that vests on the fifth day of the league year (March 16), so the Seahawks will want to decide by then whether they want him on next year's team. But if they do, they'd also look to extend him beyond that.

What's interesting to me is that this is a different setup than Darnold had last offseason, when $17.5 million of his 2026 compensation became guaranteed on the fifth day after the Super Bowl. That was a no-brainer, of course, since Seattle won the Super Bowl with him five days earlier. But if this season doesn't go as well (the Seahawks are 3-3, and only Justin Herbert has thrown more interceptions than Darnold's seven), Seattle has four more weeks to make the decision on Darnold than it did a year ago.

Fowler: It's not helping that Drew Lock has been impressive for the Seahawks, both behind the scenes and in relief of Darnold. Darnold has earned a lot of street cred with Seattle, but he must limit the turnovers, especially with the team's dominant defense.

Houston's C.J. Stroud is fueling the offseason intrigue with his excellent play. He is putting up MVP-type numbers, pacing for nearly 4,900 passing yards over a 17-game slate while registering only one interception on 219 passing attempts. Betting on himself in Year 4 should literally pay off. The Texans were willing to extend Stroud on a deal worth well above $50 million per year. But Stroud saw a bigger picture: a growing quarterback market and his place in it. Stroud and Carolina's Bryce Young both appear well-positioned for offseason negotiations. And Houston's trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. -- Stroud's teammate while at Ohio State -- amplifies the Texans' feelings on Stroud.

What's next for the Colts? Could more moves be coming?
Fowler: It feels as if everything is on the table in Indianapolis, from an eventual head coaching change to a quarterback demotion, barring an uptick in performance. Daniel Jones' play -- 30th in QBR (38.2) with 1.5 turnovers per game -- is unsustainable over a 17-game season. This situation mirrors that of the 2025 Dolphins, who fired general manager Chris Grier in October but evaluated coach Mike McDaniel over the remainder of the season, only to fire him four days after Week 18. Miami also benched a quarterback with a high-priced contract in Tua Tagovailoa late in the campaign.

The sentiment as of now is that Colts coach Shane Steichen will get more chances to state his case for the job moving forward. But typically, franchises like to synchronize their brain trust on similar timelines, often with a newly appointed general manager spearheading a search for the new coach. That might not bode well for Steichen, whose acumen never has been questioned. He'd be in the mix for head coaching jobs or primo playcaller positions in the 2027 cycle. I'm curious about your take, Dan, but I believe team owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon plans to place her stamp on the franchise in a big way over the coming months.

Graziano: I would agree that while Steichen is well-regarded and well-liked in the building, this is definitely a situation worth monitoring for potential change at the end of the season, if not sooner. Firing a GM in mid-October indicates disappointment from ownership, obviously, but it also signals the possibility of major change on the roster, maybe even in the next few weeks. The NFL trade deadline is Nov. 10 -- less than three weeks from now -- and the Colts have a very interesting roster. There were a number of veterans who could have received contract extensions this past offseason, and the only one who got one was running back Jonathan Taylor.

High-profile veteran players such as offensive lineman Quenton Nelson, defensive linemen DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart, and wide receivers Josh Downs and Keenan Allen are on contracts that expire at the end of the season. If the Colts (who are without a 2027 first-round pick as a result of last year's Sauce Gardner trade) want to try to regain some draft capital, they could look to deal some players who they don't view as part of their future. Depending on the extent of that dealing, it could get even more difficult for Steichen to win games in the second half of the campaign, which would make it harder to convince the Colts to keep him around.

Fowler: Rival teams believe Indianapolis will be open for business ahead of the trade deadline, but for now, let's take Irsay-Gordon at her word. The last sentence from her statement Monday announcing GM Chris Ballard's firing read: "We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve and win football games." That puts Indy on a three-week clock, with the Vikings, Jaguars and Cowboys on the schedule between now and Nov. 8, two days before the deadline.

If Indy can find a way to steal two wins in that slate, perhaps that affects trade plans. But this iteration of the Colts does not look poised for upsets, so perhaps change is inevitable. What Indianapolis does with Nelson will be fascinating. He's a legacy Colt, a 2018 first-round draft pick and frequent All-Pro. But the team did not aggressively pursue an extension this summer, and rarely do premier O-linemen become available at the deadline. Also, defensive tackle Jerry Tillery is a name to watch.

Graziano: The new GM hire will be the first major organizational structure move since Irsay-Gordon took over as controlling owner, and it's even more significant if it is coupled with a coaching hire. You have a team that looks as if it will be in the offseason quarterback market, but it doesn't have a first-round pick, so the Colts might have to pursue unconventional ways of fixing their biggest roster problem of the past decade. How the Colts' decision-making structure comes together will be watched very closely around the league, as Irsay-Gordon is an unknown in terms of how she wants the team to operate and could be a very different type of decision-maker than her late father.

Who is a sleeper name for the trade deadline we're not talking about enough (or at all)?
Graziano: Tampa Bay defensive tackle Vita Vea. The Buccaneers are 1-5. Vea is 31 years old, and he and the team begrudgingly came to a compromise agreement on his contract during training camp. The Bucs didn't act as if he was part of their long-term future, and if teams come looking for a big, run-stuffing defensive tackle, Tampa would be silly not to listen. He is on a minimum salary this year and is guaranteed $23 million for 2027, which would rank about 15th in terms of cap numbers for defensive tackles in the league. If you need interior D-line help right now and don't mind paying Vea $23 million next season at age 32, why not call to see what it would take to get him out of Tampa?

Fowler: Tennessee cornerback Alontae Taylor. He was widely considered the top corner in free agency, signing a three-year, $58 million deal with the Titans in March. His Week 6 benching has placed him on the radar of teams that might look to bolster the position in the next few weeks. He has struggled as an outside corner for Tennessee but is at his best as a disruptive slot closer to the action. He's 27 with good football left, so a trade could bring out his best.

Money is a hurdle: Taylor's salaries of $9.49 million in 2026 and $20.5 million in 2027 are guaranteed. Perhaps a new team could rework that money on a new deal while asking Tennessee to front some of the bill in exchange for a quality pick. Tennessee has the option to smooth things out with Taylor and solidify a role for him -- and I don't believe the Titans are floating his name right now -- but a benching typically signals that a player is expendable.

Graziano: Interesting concept, the idea of a team trading a player so soon after signing him. It kind of reminds me of the Jets trading Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline a few months after extending his contract. Sometimes, circumstances change or things don't work out as expected, so teams will pivot if the terms are favorable. A couple of other 2026 free agent signings who stand out as potentially available due to their situations not working out include Texans offensive lineman Wyatt Teller and Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen.

Fowler: One surprise name a few teams are tracking is Cincinnati edge rusher Shemar Stewart. The 2025 first-round pick is not a factor in the team's rotation right now. He has played 17 defensive snaps, well behind the total for the fourth defensive end, Cedric Johnson (83). And rookie second-rounder Cashius Howell has been impressive. Cincinnati typically doesn't move its young draft picks, but it would be surprising if the Bengals haven't received inquiries on Stewart, whose upside remains high.

Also, could a team pry safety Jessie Bates III out of Atlanta? He will be a free agent in 2027, and the Falcons are sitting at 2-4. I doubt Atlanta wants to trade him, but his value would be strong if that changes.

Which NFC East team is most likely to shake things up in the coming weeks?
Fowler: I'll start with the Eagles. They come up most often regarding potential moves over the next few weeks. The Eagles are always active, and they could execute a mini-rebuild. Defensive end Moro Ojomo, a 2027 free agent, has strong trade value, so if Philadelphia isn't going to re-sign him, it could get compensatory pick value (or better) for him now. Woolen and wide receiver Hollywood Brown are players teams are watching.

I'm not wholly convinced the Eagles will move a marquee name such as Saquon Barkley. But can they find a taker for guard Landon Dickerson, who appears disgruntled and remains on injured reserve? The Eagles have been forced to reshape their once-vaunted offensive line on the fly, and that could facilitate moves. It's also worth noting that Philly is in the middle of a quarterback shake-up due to Jalen Hurts' absence, and recently acquired Joe Milton is a name to watch. The Eagles are struggling mightily to run the ball, and Milton has mobility. He could be worth looking at soon.

Graziano: The Giants could be shaking things up at quarterback, too, should they decide to give J.J. McCarthy the start this week at Houston or after their Week 8 bye. They'd also love to alter things at running back, apparently. The new coaching staff has clearly soured on Cam Skattebo, the Giants just released Najee Harris, and it wouldn't be shocking to see them add someone from the outside or give Tyrone Tracy Jr. a bigger chance.

I'm curious to see whether Washington dips back into the wide receiver market in the wake of Terry McLaurin's injury. The Commanders are 1-4-1, which might make them seem ready to unload talent. But they're only two games out of first place, and it feels like jobs might be on the line in Washington, so they might decide they need to go for it.

Fowler: The Cowboys might have one more move in them. Perhaps that's shortsighted, given their 2-4 record. But that might as well be 4-4 in this season's NFC East climate, where no commodity is proven and Philly's transitional state has cracked the door open. As one team exec pointed out to me Tuesday, Josh Sweat to Dallas makes a lot of sense. He fits Dallas' profile, and the Cowboys need edge-rush help. Sweat's Cardinals won Sunday, but they are not contention-adjacent just yet. Sweat has been linked to the Packers, too, but Green Bay has Micah Parsons returning eventually.

Graziano: Due to prior trades, Dallas has only four picks in next year's draft and is without its second-round pick in 2028, which could make deadline dealing difficult. But the Cowboys have been uncharacteristically aggressive over the past 12 months, and they're right in the thick of the division race in spite of how poorly they've played so far. They need edge-rush help, as you pointed out, and outside of the defensive tackles, it's an extremely young defense that might benefit from a Super Bowl-winning veteran such as Sweat. The Cowboys always seem to do something this time of year, though it's possible the Joey Porter Jr. trade was their very early big in-season move.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?
Graziano: Check to see if anyone in your league dropped Vikings running back Jordan Mason when he went on injured reserve in Week 2. Veteran Aaron Jones Sr. has held the fort and taken on a large workload, but the Vikings really believed this offseason that Mason was a back who could thrive in their redesigned run game. He'll get a chance to be their lead ball carrier, whether it's this week or in the weeks to come, and Minnesota has one of the most favorable remaining schedules for fantasy running backs in the entire league.

Fowler: Snag Washington tight end Chig Okonkwo off waivers. The Terry McLaurin injury enhances Okonkwo's value. Okonkwo and Jayden Daniels seem to have easy chemistry, resulting in 11 catches for 129 yards over the past two weeks. Okonkwo caught all seven of his targets Monday in San Francisco. He's still looking for his first touchdown this season, but that's a matter of time based on the way he's playing.
