stories.headline: Ronald Araújo: 'Finding what I needed' at Liverpool
stories.summary: Ronald Araújo is convinced his loan move to Liverpool from Barcelona was what he needed.
stories.body:
Ronald Araújo is convinced his loan move to Liverpool from Barcelona was what he needed.

The Uruguay defender has scored two goals in 11 appearance for the Reds, including one in Liverpool's 4-3 win over Villarreal in the Champions League on Tuesday.

"Honestly, it's been great," Araújo told Cadena Ser after Tuesday's game when asked about his summer move to England. "I'm very, very happy, both with the win and with how well I've settled in.

"I was genuinely blown away by the people at the club, and I'm just really happy to be playing, which was the most important thing."

Araújo said is certain he made the right choice by joining Liverpool. Liverpool have a £47.2 million ($62.8m) option to make his signing permanent at the end of the campaign.

"Yes, I definitely needed that change," he said. "I was very clear about it; when the season ended and we headed to the World Cup, it was a decision I felt very sure of. I spoke with the club [Barcelona,] with [Barcelona sporting director] Deco, and with the manager, and they made it very easy for me.

"They helped me a lot. I think that here I'm finding what I needed, which was to play, to feel important, and to showcase my style of football."

Araújo has impressed playing at both right-back and centre-back under Andoni Iraola.

- Mohamed Salah key in Rio Ngumoha's development at Liverpool - Virgil van Dijk

- Alexis Mac Allister: 'Something wasn't right' under Arne Slot at Liverpool

- Electric Ngumoha jolts Liverpool back to life in comeback Champions League win

On playing more as a right-back at Liverpool, Araújo said: "They [Barcelona] used to put me there in the Clásicos and I had to face some really quick wingers."

Among those he faced in LaLiga was Real Madrid's Vinícius Júnior.

"I've always had a lot of respect for Vinícius," he said. "Our duels were always great and, at the end of the day, you grow as a player when you come up against players like that.

"It's true that I feel more like playing as a centre-back -- but this position is going to help me a great deal looking ahead to the future."

Next up, Liverpool face high-flying Brighton in the Premier League.

stories.headline: The Anthony Edwards-LaMelo Ball partnership opens with chemistry and hope
stories.summary: The new LaMelo Ball-Anthony Edwards backcourt opens the season with a lot of flash and a renewed joy in Minnesota.
stories.body:
LAMELO BALL LEANS back at the top of the key and hoists the ball toward the rim, his weight on his back feet. He's stoic as the first two fall through the net. He shoots the third as if its swish is a fait accompli.

The ball rims out and he throws his hands on his head and yells, "F---!"

Anthony Edwards stands next to him, laughing. This is his opportunity. He drills three shots in a row with ease, throwing an exaggerated fist bump in the air as the third falls through the hoop. He moves on to the next station.

It's late September, and the first day of training camp for the Minnesota Timberwolves, but most of the team has been practicing together for weeks. The final drill of the day is the classic schoolyard game: Around the World, where a player must hit three shots in a row, circling the 3-point arc. All of the Wolves' guards are competing against one another.

The next time Ball gets his chance, he is standing alone at the top of the key. He's more focused this time. His weight is shifting more toward his toes. He knocks down three in a row.

Ball moves to his right for the next station, hitting the first two and bouncing on his feet as he lets the third go. As it caroms off the rim, Ball walks around the court and pulls his shirt nearly over his head in disbelief.

"A lot of joy," Wolves veteran center Rudy Gobert says as he observes the practice environment. "The vibes are great. I think we needed that."

Despite making the Western Conference finals in two of the past three years, Minnesota overhauled its roster this summer, bringing in Ball to bolster the backcourt alongside Edwards.

It made the Wolves smaller in the process -- trading Julius Randle, their key return in the 2024 Karl-Anthony Towns trade, and fan favorite Naz Reid -- but it also made them younger. Jonathan Kuminga, 24, who was signed in the offseason, and the 26-year-old Ayo Dosunmu are expected to play key roles while fitting in with Edwards' timeline.

They hope the gamble will help them compete with the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder, the past two conference champions who have used their size to knock out the Wolves in back-to-back playoffs.

"We weren't the best version ourselves last year in the playoffs, but we also know how high the bar is in the Western Conference," Wolves president Tim Connelly said at the team's media day. "We're very aware of what we have to overcome and how difficult that task will be. And we think we're more prepared than ever."

The Wolves recognized their need to lessen Edwards' ballhandling duties, and he has been more than happy to welcome the help.

"I feel like I'm a natural two guard at heart," he said. "I never thought I could develop any point guard skills. I know Finchy [coach Chris Finch] harps on me passing the ball, but now we got LaMelo, so I'm happy."

It was important for Minnesota to inject Ball's passing ability on the court but also his energy and joy into a team their coach acknowledged often lacked both in recent years.

"We've traded moodiness for giddiness," Finch said before a preseason game at Madison Square Garden this month.

Which is why these end-of-practice shootouts are so important: They hope they're a microcosm for the season.

For as much as it's thought Ball will help Edwards on the court, the organization also believes, team sources said, that their two stars can give each other something the other doesn't have. For Ball, it's a more serious edge to go with his showmanship. And for Edwards, it's a teammate with an infectious joy whose bond, they hope, will keep their superstar happy.

"When Melo walks in here, he comes into work smiling every day and just is engaged with everybody in the building," Finch told ESPN. "Anthony's a very joyous person, and that kind of energy, he feeds off of."

"But Ant has a real seriousness to him. He has a killer mentality. They're both gym rats, so that's cool. But there is a seriousness to Ant. You can flip that switch on him in a heartbeat and he responds. And I think that's what LaMelo needs to see too."

EVERY OFFSEASON GOBERT invites his Wolves teammates to join him in Paris.

The Wolves were close to making the trip happen in the summer of 2025, but with too many scheduling conflicts, it fell apart. He extended the offer again weeks before Minnesota's second-round exit in the 2026 playoffs.

"I'll set it up," Gobert told his teammates. "You guys just have to get your plane tickets and come."

Then in July, the Wolves made their move to acquire Ball. Almost instantly, they saw renewed engagement from Edwards.

Edwards hosted Ball at his home in Minneapolis. The two began working out on the court together later that month. Edwards joked he and Ball bonded over the need to limit their profanity in postgame interviews.

"We really got the same personality, for real," Ball said.

And together, they led the push to head to Paris. They chartered a plane from Minneapolis to Paris for players in town to make the trip. Fourteen players made the trip -- only Bones Hyland, who missed for personal reasons and Donte DiVincenzo, who had surgery to repair a torn Achilles a few months earlier, were not able to attend.

"Ant and Melo did a great job hyping the guys up in the group text," Gobert told ESPN. "And then I handled the logistics. It was really, really meaningful."

Immediately after the flight, Wolves players headed to the gym for a workout. Gobert organized the team to use Clichy Hall, a venue with air conditioning, which Gobert assured his teammates is not common in France, about a block away from the Seine River.

The Wolves later floated down the river on a boat tour through the city and past the Eiffel Tower. Several players point to it as the highlight of the trip.

"It was great. It makes you want to be honest with one another," Gobert told ESPN. "It makes you want to accomplish things with one another, put the work in, do the uncomfortable things. I'm excited to see how it translates to what we're going to do this year.

"I truly believe that we care about one another and we want to see each other succeed on and off the court. We want to see each other win. And in this business, it's not common to see that."

It's the kind of camaraderie Edwards has been clamoring for over several seasons. He looked at Oklahoma City and noted how their togetherness had them playing like "15 puppets on one string." (a compliment).

He noted at media day how the Wolves wouldn't spend much time together after the season in years past. But he thought winning and building a connection began in the summer.

Now, the Wolves have a teamwide fantasy football league. Edwards and Ball are in sync with their own handshake. Their group chat has been so lively that Gobert joked he has to put them on mute.

"I think a lot of people misjudge the NBA," Edwards said at Fanatics Fest over the summer. "It's just like AAU. The closer you and your team are, the more chance y'all got to win a championship."

BALL INBOUNDS THE ball to Gobert and sprints toward him.

The score is tied with 41 seconds remaining in the first half of a preseason game between the Wolves and the Indiana Pacers.

It's Oct. 7, and the Pacers' two best defenders, Andrew Nembhard and Aaron Nesmith, are pressing full court.

Nesmith stands in front of Edwards to prevent the inbounds pass, so Ball fires it toward Gobert, who gives it right back to Ball as he runs up the court with Nembhard trailing behind him.

As Ball heads toward the basket, he draws Pacers center Ivica Zubac to stop his progress, forcing Nembhard to switch and cover Gobert as he trails the play. But Edwards keeps jogging toward the 3-point line, where he stands uncovered. Ball rifles a pass toward him from underneath the basket.

Edwards knocks it down.

It's exactly what the Wolves envisioned when they acquired Ball. They see the benefit he will have for their big men -- center Joan Beringer said he'd never gotten so many lob passes as he had during their first day of practice -- and believe forward Jaden McDaniels can make an All-Star leap this season with Ball getting him more open looks.

Last season, Edwards brought the ball up the court more than any other Wolves player, according to Genius IQ, but his 3.7 assists per game were his lowest since 2021-22. His isolation plays shot up, 14.6 per 100 possessions, a career high, per Genius IQ, and the seventh-highest total in the league.

"We needed to make the game easier for Anthony," Finch said. "There might not be a guard in the league that creates more efficient offense for his teammates than LaMelo."

Ball's teammates in Charlotte last season had an effective field goal percentage of 67.9% after he passed to them for an assist opportunity. That ranked second among 199 qualified players (McDaniels actually ranked first, but with significantly less volume than Ball).

With Ball taking on more of the on-ball duties, Edwards also says he believes he can sharpen his skills as a defender.

"I feel like the last couple years I couldn't play defense as well as I wanted to because I was bringing the ball up," Edwards said. "At times I had to score all the time. I was super tired."

Minnesota will open its season Wednesday night in Miami (7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN) in a matchup of two teams who made blockbuster trades this summer. It'll be the Wolves' chance to test the chemistry of Edwards and Ball that has looked natural during the preseason. In the four exhibition games the duo played, Ball led the team in assists in three of them and Edwards led in scoring in all of them.

The Wolves understand there will be growing pains, especially if Ball sits out time. He has played an average of 50.5 games per season in his six-year career, although his 72 games played last season were the most since 2021-22, his second year in the league.

Finch knows the team hasn't yet been tested or faced any real adversity, but the Wolves are banking on both the vibe shift and their backcourt duo to carry them through.

"LaMelo's going to make mistakes. He's just going to do it with a smile on his face," Finch told ESPN. "He's going to be one of those guys that's hard to stay mad at. Anthony's hard to stay mad at too."

stories.headline: How Brady Tkachuk (and the Senators) are preparing for his Ottawa return
stories.summary: After a summer blockbuster, the former Senators captain will be playing his first game against his old team (and its vocal fans).
stories.body:
It was a picture-perfect moment for Brady Tkachuk.

He was shoulder to shoulder with Florida Panthers general manager Bill Zito, having just concluded a news conference officially welcoming him to the organization following a trade days earlier from the Ottawa Senators. Tkachuk had pulled on his new No. 8 sweater and wore it with the satisfied grin of a cat who'd caught the canary. Of a man who had everything he asked for.

Because Tkachuk had. Asked for it, that is.

Rewind not two months before that introduction on June 23, and a very different media session was playing out with Tkachuk front and center as captain of the Senators. It was April 29, and Ottawa was four days removed from being swept by Carolina in its first-round Stanley Cup playoff series. Emotions were raw and rumors were rampant -- mainly surrounding Tkachuk.

Was his heart still with the organization that drafted him fourth overall in 2018 and signed him to a seven-year, $57.5 million contract extension in 2021 -- right before he accepted the Senators' captaincy and became the face of their franchise?

Tkachuk was insulted by the question.

"I feel like I've answered this hundreds of times," he said. "None of those things [about wanting to leave Ottawa] ever came out of my mouth. Quite honestly, it's just getting frustrating. It's becoming a distraction. I have been fully committed to this team, to this city, and it's just become a distraction and frustrating to deal with."

Tkachuk said his peace, but that mic drop was only for the cameras. Behind closed doors, he asked to be moved out of Canada's capital to join his brother, Matthew, and the two-time Stanley Cup-winning Panthers. That truth came from GM Steve Staios. He grappled with his star player asking to jump ship and then being limited in the trade process by a full no-movement clause attached to Tkachuk's contract.

There was only one place for which Tkachuk was willing to waive it. So, Staois delivered Tkachuk to the Sunshine State in a blockbuster deal June 21 that brought back a trio of first-round draft choices (two in 2026 and one in 2029) plus a 2027 second-round selection to the Senators.

When the deed was done, Staios declined to comment on Tkachuk's reasons for requesting a trade -- but the outcome was entirely driven by Tkachuk.

"He wanted to be traded," Staios said in June. "I was always fully supportive and wanted to make it work long term. I think it became clear as [last] season went on that maybe something was amiss."

Tkachuk explained himself eventually. The forward left town -- with 213 goals in 572 games -- on the wings of a social media post thanking the Ottawa fans and community for their support during his eight-year run. That sentiment fell flat in the gaping disconnect between his words and actions. Inevitably, Tkachuk would have to face the music -- in person -- and Florida's schedule had the reunion on fast-track, less than three weeks into Tkachuk's first season in new threads.

It will be no ordinary night Wednesday (7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN+), when the visiting Panthers will feel targeted in a whole different way by a fanbase riled up over Tkachuk's unceremonious departure in search of a "new chapter" he never admitted to wanting.

"There were definitely a lot of different things that happened throughout my time [in Ottawa]." Tkachuk said in the wake of the trade. "It wasn't an easy decision, it was something I took a little bit more time with than what's been [said] out there. It was a very hard decision. There's a lot more things that go into it, but for me now, just very thankful for what [the Senators] have done for me, not just as a player, but molding me into the human that I am today."

TKACHUK THE SEQUEL was a slow burn in Florida.

The first Tkachuk landing came when Matthew -- disgruntled in Calgary and unwilling to sign an extension there -- was traded to Florida in a July 2022 blockbuster. The chemistry clicked from Game 1, with Tkachuk scoring in his Panthers debut and tallying three goals and eight points through six games.

Brother Brady looked pedestrian by comparison, with zero goals and zero points for Florida heading into its seventh game of this season against Columbus.

The lack of production from Brady Tkachuk -- after willing his way onto the Panthers' roster -- led critics and comics alike to chime in on the stagnation. But then Tkachuk issued a rebuttal. In the second period against the Blue Jackets, he scored a natural hat trick to guide Florida to a 7-3 win (Matthew, of course, assisted on the trio of strikes).

Two nights later, Tkachuk was back punching in another natural hat trick in Florida's 3-2 overtime victory against Vancouver. That made him the first Panthers player to post consecutive natural hat tricks and only the third skater ever to do it.

He now had the necessary confidence boost ahead of what is sure to be a tumultuous homecoming in Ottawa.

"Today was pretty special," Tkachuk said. "It's pretty cool, but I know my goal in being here, and that's being part of something special, not just the individual stuff. It is great, but there are bigger goals out there."

Tkachuk notched the second of his momentous nights on home ice, prompting acknowledgement of the warm reception he'd enjoyed thus far.

"It's such an amazing fanbase, such amazing people here," Tkachuk said of Florida's faithful. "To feel the support from them, it meant a lot to me."

IT'S LIKELY THAT the greeting Tkachuk receives up north will be frostier. The Senators held a "Chuk Your Tkachuk" promotion in July when fans could trade in their former captain's sweater for a discount on other team merchandise. And even Ottawa's local baseball team, the Titans, hosted a "Forget Brady Day" that same month when fans could swap their Tkachuk jersey (when he still wore No. 7) for the No. 7 jersey of Titans infielder AJ Wright; 52 fans took them up on the offer.

The intermittent months of cooling off don't lessen the emotions. Tkachuk claims, at least, he's ready for anything when stepping back into the Senators' ring.

"I don't really have an expectation," Tkachuk said of the crowd reaction. "Whatever it is, it just shows how great of a fanbase it is. If it's negative, it just shows how passionate the fans are, and why I enjoyed playing in front of them. If it's positive, I'm just really grateful for my time there."

Tkachuk will make the best of what's thrown his way. He told Matthew on Tuesday's episode of their "Wingman" podcast that if any of his old No. 7 sweaters are disgruntledly tossed onto the ice during Wednesday's tilt, he will make sure they're donated to the Boys and Girls Club in Ottawa.

Clearly the reunion is on Tkachuk's mind to some degree, but his former teammates claim they're not giving it much thought.

"Brady's not really a topic of conversation in our dressing room," Nick Cousins said. "We don't really talk about it at all ... but I think it's going to be an emotional night for him."

True, because there is only one main character in this week's drama. And the anxiety over reaching a significant return game can -- like Tkachuk's ponderous start to his scoring career in Florida -- be unexpectedly delayed. It was for John Tavares.

Perhaps better than most, Tavares can appreciate and anticipate what awaits Tkachuk. Granted, Brady has Matthew to lean on when processing any emotions. But Matthew wasn't the Flames captain when he orchestrated an exit. Tavares was that for the New York Islanders when, in 2018, he passed on returning to the Islanders and left for Toronto in free agency.

Islanders fans were ruthless in attacking Tavares' decision -- the social media post of him in Leafs bedsheets as a child heralding the news of his eight-year contract didn't help matters there -- and Tavares had to eventually pay the piper in February 2019. The hostile crowd on Long Island didn't hold back, letting Tavares have it each time he touched the puck with boos and chants of "We Don't Need You" or "It's Your Bedtime," among other things.

Toronto played Edmonton at home the night before that reunion, and Tavares' focus had been trained fully on the Oilers. It wasn't until Tavares was cooling down postgame -- and was approached by former president of hockey operations Brendan Shanahan -- that the full weight of his next outing hit him.

"I remember Brendan coming up to talk to me, and just trying to help and be supportive," Tavares recalled. "And I think I realized then that going back would be something more than I was used to. I think I knew there'd be a lot of attention and noise about it, but I think it wasn't until then where, all at once, it really clicked that this was going to be something I hadn't experienced before, and there's going to be a lot of mixed emotions."

Tavares still speaks warmly about Islanders fans -- who continued taunting him during the Leafs' subsequent visits to Long Island -- and admits the support they offered during his nine-year stint was part of what made signing elsewhere so agonizing. It's much the same tone Tkachuk has tried to deliver, although he asked for the change and Tavares earned the right to make one.

Regardless, Tavares' tip is to be grateful. When the comeback inevitably feels heavy, hold on to the good memories.

"As difficult as the reception can be, if it's more on the negative side, I think just remind yourself to always acknowledge those feelings, too, because it's important," Tavares said. "Not everyone's privy to being inside your head or in your shoes, and living the ins and outs of your life, or really seeing or getting an understanding of what goes on, and what happens in terms of your career.

"Going back to a place you moved on from that meant a lot to you, and where you meant a lot to the organization and the fans, everyone's going to have their opinion. But just be appreciative of the way people believed in you. It is really meaningful if you ever get to have that."

Ottawa will have to manage its feelings, too. Coach Travis Green said his expectations over the fan response "doesn't matter at all," but it will be on Green to ensure his group isn't distracted by the extra energy.

"There will be a lot of emotion in the game and in the building. There always is when a player of that magnitude first comes back," Green said. "Whenever there's a game [like that], it's exciting. This will be a real fun game to play in. There's always some buildup the first time coming back ... but I'm not going to overthink it."

TKACHUK'S PUBLIC RATIONALE for abdicating his post in Ottawa has zeroed in on two factors: Florida's championship pedigree and the opportunity to suit up with Matthew in the NHL after successful international tournaments.

The brothers played together for Team USA at the 4 Nations Face-Off in February 2025 and then again at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics. Winning gold there -- after a runner-up finish at 4 Nations -- was an unforgettable experience that made the comedown from Ottawa's quick playoff ouster seemingly more difficult to swallow. Tkachuk had already watched Matthew win two Stanley Cups with the Panthers before going through the high of securing gold with him overseas. He wanted it all, too.

Their dad, Keith -- an NHL legend and soon-to-be Hockey Hall of Fame inductee -- couldn't fault Brady for following his heart.

"They've dreamt of playing together," Keith Tkachuk said this summer. "They had an opportunity in the Olympics and [at] the 4 Nations. They're best friends, they wanted to do this together, and fortunately, it worked out. Both parties found a way to get it done."

Still, Brady told Matthew on a June episode of their podcast his true priority in selecting Florida for his second act.

"I made this decision taking you out of it. It wasn't about you," Brady said. "You know how much I love you, but every single time after playing you guys, I was like, 'Holy cow, that team is incredible and they have a chance to win every single year.'"

At least one of Tkachuk's friends in Ottawa and on Team USA -- defenseman Jake Sanderson -- understands Tkachuk wanting to migrate down south with the Panthers, even if the call Sanderson got from Staios telling him about the trade was hard to hear.

"Looking back, I shouldn't be surprised that Brady wanted to go play with his brother," Sanderson said. "I don't think anybody should be. But to see it actually happen was crazy. He was such a big personality and leader in our room, so things will be different for sure."

Sanderson has been sidelined by an injury early this season but is projected to get back in against Florida. If all goes well, he'll be trying to keep Tkachuk from running wild in his old barn.

"It'll be a high-compete game," Sanderson said. "Obviously with Brady coming back, that's a [big thing]. But you have to separate the two and be like, we're playing the Florida Panthers. That's the most important thing."

Tage Thompson was an emergency recall for Team USA at 4 Nations but a full participant on the Olympics journey, when he saw firsthand a masterclass in brotherly bonding play out.

"Really, what you see is what you get with [Brady] and Matthew," Thompson said. "I feel like they're a wide-open book. Both really big personalities. They rile each other up and bounce off each other. So it's fun to be around. It keeps the room light, and I think you need that, especially during the season.

"It's a long regular season. There's going to be a lot of ups and downs, and anytime you can keep the room light, I think it just kind of helps focus on just a day at a time and not think about the past or way too far about the future. So they do a good job of that."

Brady has the same sort of pesky persona on the ice as Matthew -- Brady's 812 penalty minutes in 576 career games with the Senators is second most in franchise history -- that makes him as terrifying an opponent as he is a terrific teammate. It's a frustrating, fascinating dichotomy that Thompson, having experienced both sides, can appreciate and abhor.

"Brady's always been one of those guys that you absolutely hate playing against but love on your team," Thompson said. "He's a lot of fun to be around, someone that just comes to the rink and he just has fun with the game, and that's what it's all about. It doesn't really matter the circumstance or the stage, it's all about having fun.

"But then at the same time, when it's time to go out there and do your job and compete, he's one of the best at it. That's why I think guys who play with him always love him so much."

It's also another part of what Tkachuk said made parting with the Senators emotionally fraught. Tkachuk had good friends inside and outside the dressing room -- and still does. Ottawa wing Drake Batherson planned to see Tkachuk for dinner the night before Wednesday's game to catch up with a pal he couldn't fault for handling his own business.

"Guys in their careers, they are going to do whatever they are going to do," Batherson said. "It's not going to change the relationship I have with him because [he] wants to play somewhere else. We are still going to be friends."

Tkachuk's departure hurt the Senators' short-term prospects. That alone could have led to some difficult conversations before he closed the door behind him in Ottawa.

"It was a small group of people that knew," Tkachuk said of spreading the news. "I had conversations with a couple guys before. And I made some phone calls after. There's some guys that I spent eight years with. [We] went through a lot of tough times. And I think through those tough times, through the adversity, you just get so close that they're not just teammates -- they're family."

And now, it's time for the prodigal son's return.

stories.headline: How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at United States GP -- with or without Qatar, Abu Dhabi races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by 102 points in the standings with a maximum of 150 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he could be crowned champion as early as Oct. 24 at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, but the maths around that calculation are slightly complicated by question marks over the final two races of the season. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 125 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would change the maths around the championship fight, making it easier for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Austin.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli, it's too late

- Verstappen takes back-to-back wins with dominant Singapore drive

- Hamilton calls Singapore strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

Alongside Russell and Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris are still mathematically in contention for this year's championship, although the incredibly slim hopes of Leclerc and Norris would be snuffed out entirely by the cancellation of the races in the Middle East.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Austin?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Austin remain relatively slim. The Mercedes driver would need to win in Texas, with his teammate Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton finishing fifth or lower.

Such a scenario would put Antonelli 125 points ahead of Russell with 125 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Austin, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories (by that stage Antonelli would be on nine and Russell on three with five races remaining).

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli would only need to leave Austin with a lead of 100 points over his rivals.

Such a scenario would result in the following permutations:

If Antonelli wins in Austin he would be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish.
If Antonelli finishes second, he would be crowned champion if Russell doesn't win the race.
If Antonelli finishes third, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes off the podium.
If Antonelli finishes fourth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes behind him and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes fifth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fourth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes sixth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fifth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes seventh, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes sixth or lower and Hamilton does not finish in the top two.
If Antonelli finishes eighth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes seventh or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top two and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes ninth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes eighth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli fails to score, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton finishes fifth or lower and Verstappen does not win the race.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs 49 points over the remaining rounds, which could be achieved with as little as five sixth place finishes and one fifth place finish over the rest of the season.

If only five races remain, Antonelli would need just 24 points to secure the title, which would be attainable with two seventh place finishes and three eighth place finishes at the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.

stories.headline: Petr Yan vs. Merab Dvalishvili joins rare list of trilogy bouts at UFC 333
stories.summary: ESPN categorizes all 19 of the UFC's trilogies ahead of Petr Yan vs. Merab Dvalishvili 3 at UFC 333 on Saturday.
stories.body:
When men's bantamweight champion Petr Yan and former champion Merab Dvalishvili fight in the UFC 333 co-main event on Saturday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, it will be their third meeting, completing the promotion's 20th trilogy.

This weekend's headliners, featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski and undefeated challenger Movsar Evloev, will square off for the first time, but Volkanovski has already been part of a UFC trilogy. His threepeat with Max Holloway several years ago played out far differently from what will unfold in the UFC 333 co-main. That's guaranteed. (Read on to find out why.)

How fitting is it that Saturday's event is numbered 333, a coincidental acknowledgment that when the UFC deals out three of a kind, the fans end up with a winning hand. Usually.

Trilogies come in all shapes with all sizes. Many of the sport's biggest stars have been in one or more, yet at least one UFC three-fight series featured competitors newer fans probably haven't heard of. Some trilogies have had championship-level stakes in each fight, while others have been driven by nothing but a scornful rivalry that makes the fights feel no less consequential. A few trilogies have been one-sided and a couple have concluded without establishing who's better. We did the math.

Other MMA organizations have staged trilogies, and some have played out across multiple promotions, but this list sticks to the 19 all-UFC trilogies to date and sorts them by similarities and distinguishing factors.

Passing the torch
Trilogies in which the winner of the first fight was at the top of the sport, and by the third meeting the opponent was MMA's top fighter

Chuck Liddell vs. Randy Couture
Results:

UFC 43, June 6, 2003: Couture def. Liddell (TKO3) for interim light heavyweight title
UFC 52, April 16, 2005: Liddell def. Couture (KO1) for light heavyweight title
UFC 57, Feb. 4, 2006: Liddell def. Couture (KO2) for light heavyweight title

Notable: In the lead-up to their second meeting, Liddell and Couture coached against each other on the inaugural season of "The Ultimate Fighter," the reality show UFC CEO Dana White often credits with keeping the UFC in business. Through their TV appearances and contrasting fighting styles and personalities, Liddell and Couture helped catapult MMA toward the sports mainstream. Couture is one of just three fighters (along with Tito Ortiz and Matt Hughes) to compete in two UFC trilogies -- this one and a trio of fights with Vitor Belfort.

Georges St-Pierre vs. Matt Hughes
Results:

UFC 50, Oct. 22, 2004: Hughes def. St-Pierre (Sub1) for welterweight title
UFC 65, Nov. 18, 2006: St-Pierre def. Hughes (TKO2) for welterweight title
UFC 79, Dec. 29, 2007: St-Pierre def. Hughes (Sub2) for interim welterweight title

Notable: This is the only UFC trilogy to feature multiple submission finishes. Hughes won by armbar at UFC 50, and St-Pierre ended the trilogy at UFC 79 by submitting Hughes, also by armbar. When the fighters were standing, though, GSP dominated. In their second meeting, he outstruck Hughes 49-10 with two knockdowns. In the third fight, it was 97-10.

A stunning start ... and finish
Trilogies that began with a shocking KO upset, followed by the KO victim scoring two dominant wins

Cain Velasquez vs. Junior Dos Santos
Results:

UFC on Fox, Nov. 12, 2011: Dos Santos def. Velasquez (KO1) for heavyweight title
UFC 155, Dec. 29, 2012: Velasquez def. Dos Santos (UD) for heavyweight title
UFC 166, Oct. 19, 2013: Velasquez def. Dos Santos (TKO5) for heavyweight title

Notable: The first fight lasted barely a minute, as Dos Santos essentially won by one-punch knockout. The rematch and trilogy fight dramatically swung the other way. Velasquez battered JDS for the full 25 minutes of their second meeting, as reflected by one judge awarding him two 10-8 rounds. Velasquez became the first UFC fighter to reach triple-figure significant strikes (111) and double-figure takedowns (11) in a single fight.

Stipe Miocic vs. Daniel Cormier
Results:

UFC 226, July 7, 2018: Cormier def. Miocic (KO1) for heavyweight title
UFC 241, Aug. 17, 2019: Miocic def. Cormier (TKO4) for heavyweight title
UFC 252, Aug. 15, 2020: Miocic def. Cormier (UD) for heavyweight title

Notable: Cormier was light heavyweight champion when he first faced Miocic, and by crushing the heavyweight king with an uppercut, Cormier became the second UFC champ to reign in two weight classes simultaneously. Miocic bounced back in the next two fights, and his victory in the third meeting tied him with Couture for the most UFC heavyweight title-fight wins, with six.

Back and forth (and back)
Trilogies in which the winner of the first fight lost the second, then won the third -- a rarity

Randy Couture vs. Vitor Belfort
Results:

UFC 15, Oct. 17, 1997: Couture def. Belfort (TKO1)
UFC 46, Jan. 31, 2004: Belfort def. Couture (TKO1) for light heavyweight title
UFC 49, Aug. 21, 2004: Couture def. Belfort (TKO3) for light heavyweight title

Notable: Entering the first fight, Belfort was 20 years old and 4-0 as a pro -- all knockouts of a minute, 17 seconds or faster. But Couture, 34, stopped his momentum cold. When they met again six years later, Belfort won in 49 seconds after his glove scraped Couture's eye, causing a corneal abrasion that prompted the cageside doctor to stop the fight. In the third fight, Couture brutalized Belfort for three rounds before that event's doctor had seen enough. This is the only UFC trilogy in which two fights ended by doctor's stoppage.

BJ Penn vs. Matt Hughes
Results:

UFC 46, Jan. 31, 2004: Penn def. Hughes (Sub1) for welterweight title
UFC 63, Sept. 23, 2006: Hughes def. Penn (TKO3) for welterweight title
UFC 123, Nov. 20, 2010: Penn def. Hughes (KO1)

Notable: After two unsuccessful bids for the lightweight championship, Penn moved up to welterweight and won the belt in a stunning upset, ending Hughes' two-year reign and 13-fight winning streak. After Hughes won the rematch to even the score, Penn completed the trilogy in style, knocking out Hughes in 21 seconds -- the fastest finish in a UFC trilogy.

You're just flexing now
Trilogies that ended in a 3-0 sweep

Tito Ortiz vs. Ken Shamrock
Results:

UFC 40, Nov. 12, 2002: Ortiz def. Shamrock (TKO3) for light heavyweight title
UFC 61, July 8, 2006: Ortiz def. Shamrock (TKO1)
UFC Ortiz vs. Shamrock 3, Oct. 10, 2006: Ortiz def. Shamrock (TKO1)

Notable: This trilogy is unmatched in its bitter animosity, for sure, and maybe even in one-sidedness. The feud grew out of the brash Ortiz defeating fighters from Shamrock's highly regarded Lion's Den gym, then mocking that team with vulgar gestures and custom T-shirts. Ortiz and Shamrock finally met at UFC 40 amid much anticipation, and the heated buildup drove a pay-per-view buy rate double what the UFC had ever seen.

Frankie Edgar vs. BJ Penn
Results:

UFC 112, April 10, 2010: Edgar def. Penn (UD) for lightweight title
UFC 118, Aug. 28, 2010: Edgar def. Penn (UD) for lightweight title
The Ultimate Fighter 19 Finale, July 6, 2014: Edgar def. Penn (TKO3)

Notable: Penn, who had not lost a lightweight bout in eight years, was a near 8-1 betting favorite in the first fight. Even after Edgar pulled off a narrow upset, he was still the underdog entering the rematch. He won that one more clearly with three 50-45 scorecards, then completed the trilogy with a knockout. Of the UFC's 19 trilogies, 11 have ended with a finish in the third fight. But only two -- both involving Edgar -- ended with a finish after two consecutive decisions. The other was Edgar's series with Gray Maynard.

Alexander Volkanovski vs. Max Holloway
Results:

UFC 245, Dec. 14, 2019: Volkanovski def. Holloway (UD) for featherweight title
UFC 251, July 11, 2020: Volkanovski def. Holloway (SD) for featherweight title
UFC 276, July 2, 2022: Volkanovski def. Holloway (UD) for featherweight title

Notable: Just because this trilogy ended 3-0 doesn't mean Volkanovski had it easy. In the second fight, Holloway knocked him down in each of the first two rounds, forcing the champ to play catch-up. Holloway made Volkanovski work the full five rounds in all three fights. At 75 minutes of total cage time, this is the UFC's longest trilogy.

Let's call it even
Trilogies that ended at 1-1, plus a draw

Frankie Edgar vs. Gray Maynard
Results:

UFC Fight Night, April 2, 2008: Maynard def. Edgar (UD)
UFC 125, Jan. 1, 2011: Maynard vs. Edgar for lightweight title ends in split draw
UFC 136, Oct. 8, 2011: Edgar def. Maynard (KO4) for lightweight title

Notable: The second meeting produced the greatest comeback and the most memorable draw in UFC history. Maynard knocked Edgar down three times in Round 1 while piling up a 47-10 edge in strikes landed. All three judges scored it 10-8, and Edgar was so rocked that he doesn't remember anything from the rounds that followed. He "missed" a great fight. The final meeting also began badly for Edgar, but this time his comeback built toward a late knockout that emphatically evened the score.

Valentina Shevchenko vs. Alexa Grasso
Results:

UFC 285, March 4, 2023: Grasso def. Shevchenko (Sub4) for women's flyweight title
Noche UFC, Sept. 16, 2023: Shevchenko vs. Grasso for women's flyweight title ends in split draw
UFC 306, Sept. 14, 2024: Shevchenko def. Grasso (UD) for women's flyweight title

Notable: The only women's trilogy in UFC history opened with a staggering upset, as Grasso capitalized on an ill-advised spinning attack by Shevchenko to seize control and quickly lock in a choke that ended the champ's six-year unbeaten run. Grasso narrowly held on to the title in a tightly contested second fight. Shevchenko dominated the third meeting, thanks to a change in strategy. Her grappling-heavy approach produced at least one takedown in each of the five rounds, 16 minutes of ground control and a trio of 50-45 scorecards.

Remember me?
Trilogies with at least seven years between fights

Dustin Poirier vs. Max Holloway
Results:

UFC 143, Feb. 4, 2012: Poirier def. Holloway (Sub1) for interim lightweight title
UFC 236, April 13, 2019: Poirier def. Holloway (UD)
UFC 318, July 19, 2025: Holloway def. Poirier (UD) for BMF title

Notable: The first fight was Holloway's UFC debut at 20 years old, and their final meeting 13 years later was Poirier's retirement fight. By winning that third bout, Holloway became the first fighter to win a UFC trilogy after losing the first two matchups.

Leon Edwards vs. Kamaru Usman
Results:

UFC on Fox, Dec. 19, 2015: Usman def. Edwards (UD)
UFC 278, Aug. 20, 2022: Edwards def. Usman (KO5) for welterweight title
UFC 268, March 18, 2023: Edwards def. Usman (MD) for welterweight title

Notable: Usman was 58 seconds from going up 2-0 in this series when an Edwards head kick out of nowhere changed everything. Usman had won 15 fights in a row and was on the verge of tying Anderson Silva's record for the longest UFC win streak at the time. Since that shocking defeat, he's gone 1-3, including another loss to Edwards.

No gold, just (a little) glory
Trilogies in which no championships were on the line

Sam Stout vs. Spencer Fisher
Results:

UFC 58, March 4, 2006: Stout def. Fisher (SD)
UFC Fight Night, June 12, 2007: Fisher def. Stout (UD)
UFC on FX, June 22, 2012: Stout def. Fisher (UD)

Notable: The first meeting was Stout's UFC debut, and apparently both fighters were just warming up. The rematch and trilogy fight each earned fight of the night bonuses. The third meeting had an added emotional element for Stout, as it was his first fight after the death of his coach and brother-in-law, Shawn Tompkins.

Forrest Griffin vs. Tito Ortiz
Results:

UFC 59, April 15, 2006: Ortiz def. Griffin (SD)
UFC 106, Nov. 21, 2009: Griffin def. Ortiz (SD)
UFC 148, July 7, 2012: Griffin def. Ortiz (UD)

Notable: Both competitors were 205-pound champions, just not during any of their three meetings. All three fights happened after Ortiz's title reign from 2000 to 2003. The first fight was before Griffin became champ in 2008, and the other two were after he lost the belt later that same year. The trilogy fight was Griffin's career finale and Ortiz's final UFC appearance.

Charles Oliveira vs. Nik Lentz
Results:

UFC on Versus, June 26, 2011: Oliveira vs. Lentz ends in no contest
UFC Fight Night, May 30, 2015: Oliveira def. Lentz (Sub3)
UFC Fight Night, May 18, 2019: Oliveira def. Lentz (TKO2)

Notable: The first bout appeared to end with an Oliveira rear-naked choke in Round 2, but the Pennsylvania State Athletic Commission ruled that Oliveira had landed an illegal knee and overturned the result to a no-contest. The bout earned both men fight of the night bonuses, as did the second fight.

Dustin Poirier vs. Conor McGregor
Results:

UFC 178, Sept. 27, 2014: McGregor def. Poirier (TKO1)
UFC 257, Jan. 23, 2021: Poirier def. McGregor (TKO2)
UFC 264, July 10, 2021: Poirier def. McGregor (TKO1)

Notable: This rivalry could have fit in the "Remember me?" category because of the seven-year gap between the first and second bouts. But what truly makes this trilogy stand apart from all others is McGregor's star power. He headlined the seven highest-selling pay-per-views in UFC history, and only his bouts with Khabib Nurmagomedov and Nate Diaz outsold his two meetings with Poirier in 2021. McGregor suffered the first two knockout losses of his MMA career in those bouts, the second finish coming by doctor's stoppage after he broke his left tibia and fibula.

Three is not enough?
The only UFC tetralogy -- plus 75% of another

Brandon Moreno vs. Deiveson Figueiredo
Results:

UFC 256, Dec. 12, 2020: Moreno vs. Figueiredo for men's flyweight title ends in majority draw
UFC 263, June 12, 2021: Moreno def. Figueiredo (Sub3) for men's flyweight title
UFC 270, Jan. 22, 2022: Figueiredo def. Moreno (UD) for men's flyweight title
UFC 283, Jan. 21, 2023: Moreno def. Figueiredo (TKO3) for men's flyweight title

Notable: These two flyweights squeezed in four fights over 25 months, faster than many two-fight series. Moreno and Figueiredo each produced heart-pounding moments throughout the four fights, and together they landed exactly 700 strikes. The second fight represented a memorable accomplishment for Moreno when he became the first Mexico-born UFC champion.

Tim Sylvia vs. Andrei Arlovski
Results:

UFC 51, Feb. 5, 2005: Arlovski def. Sylvia (Sub1) for interim heavyweight title
UFC 59, April 15, 2006: Sylvia def. Arlovski (TKO1) for heavyweight title
UFC 61, July 8, 2006: Sylvia def. Arlovski (UD) for heavyweight title
One FC 5, Aug. 31, 2012: Sylvia vs. Arlovski ends no contest in One Championship

Notable: The first fight lasted 47 seconds, with Arlovski's quick knockdown leading to a leg-lock finish. Arlovski nearly repeated the feat in the rematch, dropping Sylvia halfway through Round 1. But after a wobbly Sylvia got back to his feet and Arlovski moved in for a finish, Sylvia caught him with a short uppercut to even the score. Their final UFC meeting turned into a tactical, tentative sparring session, as one might expect from a matchup where each fighter had already felt the other's power. Also as expected, the ornery crowd was unimpressed.
